cards.front: The kidney's mineralocorticoid receptor binds cortisol as tightly as aldosterone, and plasma carries far more cortisol. Why does renal sodium transport still follow aldosterone?
cards.back: An enzyme in the kidney inactivates most of the cortisol near the receptor.
cards.quote: The short answer: an enzyme in the kidney inactivates cortisol near the receptor

cards.front: State the three-step rule for reading any adrenal state, in its required order.
cards.back: 1. Enzymes: a missing enzyme lowers everything after it and backs up the substance just before it. 2. Receptors: what can the steroids now present do at a receptor? 3. Loops: only then let the controls respond.
cards.why: The rule predicts the direction of steady-state changes compared with a healthy person, not their size, speed or symptoms.
cards.quote: A missing enzyme lowers everything after it and backs up the substance just before it.

cards.front: Name the three zones of the adult human adrenal cortex, outer to inner, and the main product of each.
cards.back: Glomerulosa: aldosterone (mineralocorticoid). Fasciculata: cortisol (glucocorticoid). Reticularis: DHEA and androstenedione, mostly weak androgens.
cards.quote: The outer cortex has three zones that make steroids from cholesterol: a salt hormone (aldosterone), a fuel hormone (cortisol) and androgen precursors.

cards.front: The slow step shared by every adrenal cortical zone is cholesterol to pregnenolone, catalysed by the mitochondrial {{c1::side-chain cleavage enzyme (CYP11A1)}}.
cards.quote: Cholesterol is cut to pregnenolone by the mitochondrial side-chain cleavage enzyme (CYP11A1).
cards.section: One trunk, three branches: the cortical zones

cards.front: How does ACTH speed the slow step of adrenal steroid synthesis, within minutes and over days?
cards.back: Within minutes: more cholesterol delivery to CYP11A1 via the StAR protein, which carries cholesterol into the mitochondrion. Over days: induction of the pathway's enzymes.
cards.quote: within minutes by raising cholesterol delivery to the enzyme (through the StAR protein, which moves cholesterol to the inner mitochondrial membrane where the enzyme sits), and over days by inducing the pathway's enzymes.
cards.section: One trunk, three branches: the cortical zones

cards.front: In the adult human adrenal, why can the zona glomerulosa make aldosterone but not cortisol?
cards.back: It alone has aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2), and it lacks 17-alpha-hydroxylase, which the route to cortisol needs.
cards.quote: Lacks 17-alpha-hydroxylase, so it cannot make cortisol.
cards.section: One trunk, three branches: the cortical zones

cards.front: What are the two jobs of CYP17A1, and which adrenal product needs each?
cards.back: 17-alpha-hydroxylation (needed for cortisol) and 17,20-lyase side-chain cutting (needed for androgens). The reticularis uses the lyase activity strongly.
cards.quote: CYP17A1 has two jobs: adding a 17-hydroxyl group (needed for cortisol) and cutting the side chain (needed for androgens).
cards.section: One trunk, three branches: the cortical zones

cards.front: In the adrenal cortex, 21-hydroxylase lies on the routes to cortisol and {{c1::aldosterone}}, not to the androgens.
cards.quote: And 21-hydroxylase lies on the routes to cortisol and aldosterone, not to the androgens.
cards.section: One trunk, three branches: the cortical zones

cards.front: In the fasciculata: 17-alpha-hydroxylase gives 17-hydroxyprogesterone; 21-hydroxylase gives {{c1::11-deoxycortisol}}; 11-beta-hydroxylase gives cortisol.
cards.quote: Fasciculata: 17-alpha-hydroxylase gives 17-hydroxyprogesterone; 21-hydroxylase gives 11-deoxycortisol; 11-beta-hydroxylase gives cortisol.
cards.section: One trunk, three branches: the cortical zones

cards.front: In the glomerulosa, 21-hydroxylase makes {{c1::11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC)}}, which aldosterone synthase converts through corticosterone to aldosterone.
cards.quote: 21-hydroxylase makes 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC); aldosterone synthase converts DOC through corticosterone to aldosterone.
cards.section: One trunk, three branches: the cortical zones

cards.front: What do adrenal chromaffin cells release, and what triggers the release?
cards.back: Adrenaline and noradrenaline into the blood (about four-fifths adrenaline in adult humans). Preganglionic sympathetic acetylcholine acting on nicotinic receptors depolarizes them.
cards.quote: which arise from the neural crest, release adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (norepinephrine) into the blood.
cards.section: The medulla

cards.front: Why might blood draining from the adrenal cortex into the medulla favour adrenaline over noradrenaline?
cards.back: The glucocorticoid-rich blood supports PNMT, the enzyme that converts noradrenaline to adrenaline (shown mainly in rats).
cards.quote: this glucocorticoid-rich blood supports PNMT, the enzyme that converts noradrenaline to adrenaline.
cards.section: The medulla

cards.front: A drug blocks nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at autonomic ganglia. What happens to adrenal medullary catecholamine release during sympathetic activation, and why?
cards.back: It falls. Chromaffin cells are a modified sympathetic ganglion, released by preganglionic acetylcholine acting on nicotinic receptors.
cards.quote: Preganglionic sympathetic fibres release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors of chromaffin cells, which depolarize and release catecholamines within seconds
cards.section: The medulla

cards.front: Which receptor does ACTH bind on adrenal cortical cells, and how does it signal?
cards.back: The MC2 receptor (melanocortin 2), a G-protein-coupled receptor acting through Gs, cAMP and PKA; mainly on fasciculata and reticularis cells.
cards.quote: It is a G-protein-coupled receptor that signals through Gs and cyclic AMP (cAMP and PKA).
cards.section: The ACTH loop: cortisol and the androgens

cards.front: What are the main controls of aldosterone secretion in humans, and why does loss of pituitary ACTH leave aldosterone largely intact?
cards.back: Angiotensin II and a rise in plasma potassium. ACTH stimulates aldosterone less, and with continuous exposure that effect fades.
cards.quote: ACTH stimulates it too, but less, and with continuous exposure that effect fades
cards.section: The second loop: angiotensin II and potassium drive aldosterone

cards.front: Trace the chain from a rise in plasma potassium to aldosterone synthesis in a glomerulosa cell.
cards.back: Potassium channels dominate resting conductance, so the cell sits near E_K. Higher plasma K+ raises E_K and depolarizes the cell; voltage-gated calcium channels open; calcium drives aldosterone synthase.
cards.why: Angiotensin II reaches the same result by closing potassium channels through its AT1 receptor.
cards.quote: A rise in plasma potassium moves that equilibrium potential up and depolarizes the cell.
cards.section: The second loop: angiotensin II and potassium drive aldosterone

cards.front: A mutation makes a glomerulosa potassium channel leak sodium inward at rest. Predict aldosterone, renin and plasma potassium.
cards.back: Aldosterone up, renin down, potassium normal or low. The leak depolarizes the cell as if K+ were high, so aldosterone is made even with low angiotensin II; sodium retention raises pressure and suppresses renin; K+ secretion rises.
cards.quote: Sodium leaking in depolarizes the cell, as if potassium were high.
cards.section: The second loop: angiotensin II and potassium drive aldosterone

cards.front: Recurrent KCNJ5 potassium-channel mutations appeared in 8 of 22 aldosterone-producing adenomas, present in tumor but not blood; in a cultured kidney cell line the mutant channels conducted sodium and depolarized the cells. What do these results show, and what do they not show?
cards.back: They show recurrent, somatic mutations that are depolarizing. They do not show that all primary aldosteronism has this cause, that a cell line behaves like a glomerulosa cell, or why the cells proliferate.
cards.quote: Recurrent mutations in KCNJ5, a potassium channel gene, appeared in 8 of 22 adenomas and were somatic: in the tumor, not the blood.
cards.section: The second loop: angiotensin II and potassium drive aldosterone

cards.front: A patient whose aldosterone-producing adenoma carries a sodium-leaking potassium-channel mutation is given a drug that lowers angiotensin II. Predict whether aldosterone falls much, and why.
cards.back: Little. The mutant cells are depolarized regardless, so calcium channels stay open and aldosterone is made even when angiotensin II is low.
cards.why: Rests on the voltage-sensor chain: depolarization, not angiotensin II itself, opens the calcium channels that drive aldosterone synthase.
cards.quote: Calcium channels open and aldosterone is made even when angiotensin II is low.
cards.section: The second loop: angiotensin II and potassium drive aldosterone

cards.front: Why is aldosterone in suspected primary aldosteronism read against renin rather than alone?
cards.back: Aldosterone made without regard to renin suppresses renin. The signature is aldosterone high for that suppressed renin (raised aldosterone-to-renin ratio), even when aldosterone itself sits near the reference range.
cards.why: Potassium is normal in many patients, so it is not a reliable marker.
cards.quote: the signature is aldosterone that is high for a suppressed renin (a raised aldosterone-to-renin ratio)
cards.section: The second loop: angiotensin II and potassium drive aldosterone

cards.front: Aldosterone is made without limit in primary aldosteronism. Why is the patient not edematous?
cards.back: Volume expands only modestly: the higher pressure raises sodium excretion (pressure natriuresis) until output matches intake. This return to balance is mineralocorticoid escape; the hypertension is the cost.
cards.quote: The higher pressure raises sodium excretion (pressure natriuresis) until output matches intake again.
cards.section: The second loop: angiotensin II and potassium drive aldosterone

cards.front: Summarize cortisol's actions on fuel metabolism.
cards.back: It raises liver glucose release after a meal, reduces glucose uptake by muscle and fat (appearing to reflect insulin resistance), raises palmitate appearance (suggesting lipolysis), and increases proteolysis, whose amino acids feed gluconeogenesis. Insulin and glucagon also changed, so not every effect is direct. Net: more glucose supply, less use, opposing insulin.
cards.quote: Cortisol thus raises glucose supply and lowers its use by muscle and fat, opposing insulin
cards.section: Cortisol shifts fuel, restrains inflammation and supports pressure

cards.front: A person with type 1 diabetes on a fixed insulin dose is given extra cortisol (hydrocortisone) for several days. Predict blood glucose, and give the reasons.
cards.back: Glucose tends to rise. Cortisol raises liver glucose release, lowers uptake by muscle and fat, and increases proteolysis feeding gluconeogenesis, opposing insulin.
cards.quote: Those amino acids feed gluconeogenesis (integration of metabolism).
cards.section: Cortisol shifts fuel, restrains inflammation and supports pressure

cards.front: How does cortisol restrain inflammation at the level of gene control?
cards.back: Through the glucocorticoid receptor, a ligand-activated transcription factor: it inhibits NF-kappa-B activation (partly by inducing I-kappa-B-alpha, varying by cell type) and binds NF-kappa-B and AP-1 directly.
cards.quote: Cortisol acts through the glucocorticoid receptor, a ligand-activated transcription factor (nuclear receptors).
cards.section: Cortisol shifts fuel, restrains inflammation and supports pressure

cards.front: Name the two routes by which cortisol supports blood pressure.
cards.back: Part of the support is thought to be permissive (keeps vascular smooth muscle responsive to noradrenaline and angiotensin II). A second route: cortisol escaping the kidney guard enzyme acts on the mineralocorticoid receptor and retains sodium.
cards.quote: Part of cortisol's support of pressure is thought to be permissive: it keeps vascular smooth muscle responsive to noradrenaline and angiotensin II.
cards.section: Cortisol shifts fuel, restrains inflammation and supports pressure

cards.front: Paired halves of a toad bladder are mounted as isolated sheets; one half gets aldosterone. After about an hour its short-circuit current rises above its partner's, and tracers confirm net sodium transport. What does this show, and what does the pairing control for?
cards.back: Aldosterone acts directly on the epithelium, with a delay; no systemic intermediary is needed in this preparation. Pairing removes differences between animals.
cards.why: The delay suggested, without proving, new protein synthesis. It did not show which mammalian nephron segment responds.
cards.quote: That ruled in a direct, delayed action on the epithelium and ruled out, in this preparation, a systemic intermediary
cards.section: Aldosterone acts on the epithelium itself, and an enzyme guards its receptor

cards.front: In an Ussing-type short-circuit experiment, why does the short-circuit current equal net active ion transport?
cards.back: With identical solutions on both sides and the voltage clamped at zero, nothing drives ions passively, so the current is net active transport, provided one ion carries it.
cards.quote: With the same Ringer solution on both sides and no voltage, nothing drives ions passively
cards.section: Aldosterone acts on the epithelium itself, and an enzyme guards its receptor

cards.front: Paired epithelial halves each expose 0.50 cm2. After aldosterone, the treated half carries 54 microamperes of short-circuit current and the control 18 microamperes. Sodium carries all net current. F = 96,485 C per mol. What is the aldosterone-induced extra sodium transport per cm2 per hour?
cards.back: Extra current 54 - 18 = 36 x 10^-6 C per s. Divide by F: 3.73 x 10^-10 mol per s. Times 3,600 s: 1.34 micromol per h. Divide by 0.50 cm2: about 2.69 micromol per cm2 per h.
cards.quote: sodium flux (mol per s) = current (C per s) / F, with F = 96,485 C per mol
cards.section: Aldosterone acts on the epithelium itself, and an enzyme guards its receptor

cards.front: An epithelial sheet of 1.00 cm2, short-circuited with identical solutions on both sides, transports net sodium at 1.00 micromol per cm2 per hour, and sodium is the only ion moving. What short-circuit current should be measured? (F = 96,485 C per mol)
cards.back: Flux = 1.00 x 10^-6 mol / 3,600 s = 2.78 x 10^-10 mol per s. Current = flux x F = 2.68 x 10^-5 C per s, about 26.8 microamperes.
cards.quote: C per s divided by C per mol gives mol per s.
cards.section: Aldosterone acts on the epithelium itself, and an enzyme guards its receptor

cards.front: The extra short-circuit current after a hormone is converted to sodium flux by dividing by F, but tracers later show another ion carried part of that current. Is the sodium estimate too high or too low?
cards.back: Too high. Dividing current by F counts all net charge movement as sodium; that is why tracer fluxes are needed to confirm which ion carries it.
cards.quote: If another ion carried part of the current, step 2 would overstate sodium transport; hence the tracers.
cards.section: Aldosterone acts on the epithelium itself, and an enzyme guards its receptor

cards.front: An isolated toad-bladder epithelium responds to aldosterone at about 670 times an illustrative adult plasma aldosterone concentration. What can and cannot be concluded about physiology?
cards.back: It shows the epithelium can respond to aldosterone directly; it does not show that it responds at physiological concentrations.
cards.quote: The classic shows that the epithelium can respond, not that it responds at physiological concentrations.
cards.section: Crabbé's method, and his concentration

cards.front: In adult human plasma, about what fraction of cortisol is protein-bound, and to which protein mainly?
cards.back: About 90 percent, mostly to corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG, transcortin). On the free hormone hypothesis only the unbound fraction acts; aldosterone binds CBG weakly.
cards.quote: In adult human plasma about 90 percent of cortisol is protein-bound, mostly to corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG, also called transcortin).
cards.section: The guard enzyme: why cortisol does not take the receptor

cards.front: Which enzyme guards the mineralocorticoid receptor in the kidney, colon and parotid, and what reaction does it catalyse?
cards.back: 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (type 2 in epithelia): it converts cortisol to inactive cortisone. Aldosterone escapes this conversion.
cards.quote: 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (11-beta-HSD) in targets such as kidney, colon and parotid protects them by converting cortisol to inactive cortisone.
cards.section: The guard enzyme: why cortisol does not take the receptor

cards.front: In severe Cushing syndrome, cortisol overwhelms the kidney's guard enzyme. Apart from cortisol's other effects, predict sodium, plasma potassium and renin.
cards.back: Sodium retained, potassium lowered, renin suppressed. Cortisol occupies the mineralocorticoid receptor itself; the retained sodium expands volume, which suppresses renin.
cards.quote: The excess cortisol gets past the enzyme and acts on the mineralocorticoid receptor itself, retaining sodium and lowering potassium.
cards.section: The guard enzyme: why cortisol does not take the receptor

cards.front: The mineralocorticoid receptor binds cortisol and aldosterone with equal affinity. Free aldosterone is 0.15 nmol per L and free cortisol 20 nmol per L. To what local cortisol concentration must the guard enzyme lower cortisol for aldosterone to hold 75 percent of occupied receptors, and what fold cut is that?
cards.back: With equal affinity, share = share of free concentrations. 0.15 / (0.15 + C) = 0.75 gives C = 0.05 nmol per L, a 20 / 0.05 = 400-fold cut.
cards.quote: With equal affinity, each steroid's share of the occupied receptors equals its share of the two free concentrations.
cards.section: How much does the guard enzyme have to do?

cards.front: Two hypertensive adults both have low renin and low potassium. In one, aldosterone is high for that renin; in the other, aldosterone is low. Give a cause consistent with each, and the rule that separates them.
cards.back: High: primary aldosteronism (autonomous aldosterone). Low: another steroid acting on the mineralocorticoid receptor, such as cortisol past a blocked or swamped guard enzyme (liquorice, severe Cushing), or DOC in 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency.
cards.why: The renin loop measures volume and pressure, not which hormone caused them, so aldosterone follows the suppressed renin unless it is made autonomously.
cards.quote: The renin loop measures volume and pressure, not which hormone caused them, which is also why aldosterone is always read against renin.
cards.section: One case all the way through: 21-hydroxylase deficiency

cards.front: In 21-hydroxylase deficiency, which steroid piles up just before the block and serves as the screening marker?
cards.back: 17-hydroxyprogesterone.
cards.quote: Cortisol and aldosterone fall, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone, the substrate just before the block, piles up; it is the screening marker.
cards.section: One case all the way through: 21-hydroxylase deficiency

cards.front: Why do adrenal androgens rise, and the gland enlarge, in 21-hydroxylase deficiency?
cards.back: Low cortisol releases the brake on ACTH. ACTH drives the shared trunk, and the extra flow spills into the androgen branch, which does not need 21-hydroxylase. Long ACTH drive causes the hyperplasia.
cards.quote: ACTH drives the trunk of the pathway, and the extra flow spills into the androgen branch, which does not need 21-hydroxylase.
cards.section: One case all the way through: 21-hydroxylase deficiency

cards.front: Why does classic salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency cause salt loss, high renin and high potassium?
cards.back: The block comes before DOC, so no precursor replaces the missing aldosterone; backed-up progesterone and 17-hydroxyprogesterone weakly antagonize the receptor. Sodium is lost, volume falls, renin rises, potassium is retained.
cards.quote: the block comes before DOC (11-deoxycorticosterone, the aldosterone precursor), so no precursor stands in for the missing aldosterone
cards.section: One case all the way through: 21-hydroxylase deficiency

cards.front: A child lacks 11-beta-hydroxylase and is retaining sodium and hypertensive. Why is plasma aldosterone low rather than high?
cards.back: DOC piles up before the block and is itself a mineralocorticoid (step two). Its sodium retention expands volume, which suppresses renin; aldosterone follows angiotensin II, so it falls (step three).
cards.why: Reading the salt retention as aldosterone's work skips step two; the loops must be run last.
cards.quote: The expanded volume suppresses renin, and because aldosterone follows angiotensin II, aldosterone falls too
cards.section: One case all the way through: 21-hydroxylase deficiency

cards.front: Why does primary adrenal insufficiency darken the skin while central (pituitary) insufficiency does not?
cards.back: In primary insufficiency, low cortisol raises ACTH, and ACTH and related peptides from its precursor POMC darken skin and mucosa. In central insufficiency ACTH itself is lost.
cards.quote: high ACTH and related peptides from its precursor (POMC) darken skin and mucosa
cards.section: The rest of the table

cards.front: Two patients have high cortisol: one from an adrenal adenoma, one from an ectopic ACTH-secreting tumor. Predict ACTH and adrenal androgens in each.
cards.back: Adenoma: ACTH suppressed, androgens down, since the androgen-making zone goes quiet with ACTH. Ectopic ACTH: ACTH up or normal, androgens up or high-normal with cortisol.
cards.quote: cortisol is made autonomously, so ACTH is suppressed and the androgen-making zone goes quiet with it.
cards.section: The rest of the table

cards.front: {{c1::Cushing disease}} is only the pituitary form of Cushing syndrome.
cards.quote: Cushing disease is only the pituitary form of Cushing syndrome.
cards.section: The rest of the table

cards.front: Suppose a drug fully blocks adrenal 17-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP17A1). Using the three-step rule, predict cortisol, adrenal androgens, ACTH, DOC, renin and blood pressure.
cards.back: Cortisol and androgens down (both need CYP17A1). ACTH up, driving the trunk into the only open branch: DOC and corticosterone pile up. DOC is a mineralocorticoid, so sodium retention and volume expansion tend to suppress renin, and pressure tends to rise.
cards.why: Rests on: a missing enzyme lowers what follows; extra ACTH-driven flow leaves through any branch still open; DOC is itself a mineralocorticoid.
cards.quote: ACTH rises when cortisol falls and drives the shared trunk of the pathway (the tree comes next), so extra flow leaves through any branch still open.

cards.front: Kidney mineralocorticoid receptors bind aldosterone and corticosterone equally, yet aldosterone controls renal sodium transport. To test whether local enzyme inactivation keeps the receptor for aldosterone, give one in vivo intervention, its predicted result, and one control.
cards.back: Block 11-beta-HSD (carbenoxolone or glycyrrhetinic acid): corticosterone should now occupy kidney receptors, with sodium retained and potassium excreted. Controls: vehicle; inhibitor without glucocorticoid; a glucocorticoid the enzyme cannot inactivate.
cards.quote: Block the enzyme (11-beta-HSD) with carbenoxolone or glycyrrhetinic acid from liquorice.
cards.section: Design problem
